item.title: Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office
item.description:

Venezuela to repeal law that bans opposition figures from office

It comes a month after opposition leader Maria Corina Machado returned to Venezuela.

Venezuela will repeal a law that prohibits opposition figures from office, National Assembly Chief Jorge Rodriguez has announced.

The legislation, approved in 2024 and criticised for enabling political persecution, targeted those who promoted or supported sanctions against the country.

“That law responded to a very specific moment in a particular situation that Venezuela was going through,” Rodriguez said on Thursday.

The law was passed just after fraught elections which the then-incumbent Nicolas Maduro ultimately won amid widespread allegations of fraud.

An interim government headed by Delcy Rodriguez, the parliamentary chief’s sister, has run Venezuela since Maduro’s abduction by US forces in January. Delcy Rodriguez promised in September during a speech at the United Nations that the South American country will hold free and fair elections, without setting a date.

Since then, the US-backed government has been in political transition talks with parts of the opposition selected by Washington. That dialogue had reached an agreement to review several laws, including the one up for repeal now, according to Jorge Rodriguez.

Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado shook up Venezuelan politics with her surprise return from exile last month. Machado won an opposition primary in 2023 to take on Maduro in the following year’s election, but she was legally barred from running. The Nobel Peace Prize laureate is widely expected to run for office in the event of an election, despite her exclusion from transition talks.

Despite being shut out, on Thursday Machado launched a system of neighbourhood assemblies aiming to gather proposals for a future government programme and democratic transition. The assemblies are expected to bring together over a million people over several months, according to Machado’s team.

“We listened to neighbours who are breaking down barriers that many thought were impossible, debating the issues that will lay the foundations for the Venezuela to come,” Machado said on social media on Thursday after the meetings. “We are designing the transition to democracy, the Venezuelan way.”

Around 2,000 meetings with residents were organised in Venezuela and abroad on the first day of the initiative, her team told the AFP news agency.

Nineteen questions are asked during the assembly, with responses fed into a digital platform. Issues of national interest range from dates for the presidential election to changes in the justice, education, health, wage and pension systems, as well as the role of the public and private sectors.

OpenAI countersues Apple over trade secrets as AI race heats up

Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition.

OpenAI has sued Apple, accusing the Big Tech giant of stealing its trade secrets and blocking its access to hardware suppliers after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

The ChatGPT maker filed counterclaims in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.

Apple and OpenAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.

Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for talent and proprietary technology.

In July, Apple sued OpenAI and two former employees, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner’s foray into consumer hardware. OpenAI has denied those allegations.

The litigation sets up a battle over who will control future AI devices that may not use traditional apps or operating systems — devices which, if successful, would direct consumer attention away from Apple’s best-selling iPhone. Analysts believe OpenAI is working on a phone or other device of its own.

Putin unveils new Russian nuclear-powered submarine with hypersonic weapons

The Kremlin plans to expand its naval fleet with five new nuclear submarines by 2030.

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has unveiled a new nuclear-powered submarine, which Moscow claims is the first equipped with Russian Zircon hypersonic missiles.

The Russians say they will add five more nuclear submarines to the country’s fleet by 2030.

Putin attended the flag-raising ceremony aboard the Perm at the Sevmash shipyard in the northwestern city of Severodvinsk on Friday, marking the submarine’s formal transfer to the navy, according to video released by the Kremlin.

“Russia is one of the few countries in the world capable of building powerful nuclear submarines of this kind, weapons with global reach and significance,” he said.

Nuclear-powered subs are a key part of Russia’s nuclear deterrent because their ability to operate covertly underwater ensures a retaliatory strike capability in the event of an attack.

Putin said the navy will receive five more submarines by 2030, including three Yasen-M class, the same as the Perm. They can operate in “any part of the world’s oceans” while carrying a range of cruise missiles, he added.

Putin also stated that Russia intends to continue modernising its navy and expressed confidence that all plans to build a powerful naval force will be implemented in full and on time.

item.title: Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, clear detail

Canada: Supreme Court largely upholds Quebec secularism bill

November 27, 2026

Quebec's government passed Bill 21 to ban religious symbols for public servants, arguing it was necessary to protect its secularist society. Critics argue the bill weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants.

However, it ruled that provincial lawmakers should be allowed to wear religious symbols in the legislature, Quebec's National Assembly.

Quebec's government passed the bill, known as Bill 21, in 2019, arguing it was necessary to protect its secular society.

Under the law, anyone receiving public services like teachers and police officers has the right to do so without being exposed to overt religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans and yarmulkes.

What did the Supreme Court say about the law?

Chief Justice Richard Wagner said that the law "is rooted in Quebec's legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the (secularism) of the state in a free and democratic society."

Mathieu Levesque, the interim the right-wing Quebecois nationalist Future Quebec Coalition (CAQ) that passed the bill, hailed it as a "victory" for the French-speaking province.

"This is a victory for the Quebec nation and for [CAQ], whose actions have today been fully validated," he said.

CAQ ruled Quebec from in two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026, after which it failed to enter parliament and the pro-independence center-left Parti Quebecois (PQ), which also supported Bill 21, formed government.

The case was seen as a major test of how far provinces can go in defying provisions of the federal constitution by invoking the "notwithstanding clause," which effectively allows provincial governments to pass laws that may breach Canada's constitution.

Quebec invoked the clause when passing the secularism bill, known as Bill 21, expecting it to be challenged over constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion.

Critics argue secularism bill weakens rights protections

Critics have argued that the bill unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens legal protections for fundamental rights.

"This decision is an unrestricted license for every government in this country to pass legislation taking away the fundamental freedoms and the legal rights of every Canadian ," Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.

He said the law forced many Muslim women to stop working as teachers or even prevented them from volunteering in schools.

Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo, was cited by Reuters as saying that the law amounted to "Islamophobia as a state policy."

Capsized tanker carrying 7,000 tonnes of diesel to be towed away from Ibiza

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.

All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.

There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.

The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".

Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".

"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.

The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.

Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.

Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.

Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".

"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.

Regional emergencies director Pablo GÃ¡rriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.

The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.

Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.

Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.

More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

“His main political platform is to say, I am not Sánchez, I am the opposite of Sánchez.” As Spain heads to the polls, what do Alberto Núñez Feijóo's campaign and political career tell us about the kind of prime minister he might become? Javier Carbonell, Policy Analyst at the European Politics and Institutions Programme and lecturer at Sciences Po in Paris, joins Gavin Lee to break down the Popular Party leader's efforts to avoid the mistakes of 2023 and keep right-wing voters mobilised without galvanising the left.

Carbonell explains the apparent paradox of Spain's strong macroeconomic performance and the difficulties many Spaniards face in their daily lives. “People still feel that their salaries are not enough to cover the cost of living.” Addressing the housing crisis, he acknowledges a problem he knows personally: “As young people, we are really, really struggling to find a house. I include myself in there.” Yet he believes pensions and pensioners will ultimately carry greater electoral weight.

What about Feijóo himself? Carbonell describes a traditional party politician whose lack of charisma is, in his view, part of his appeal. He discusses the controversy surrounding Feijóo's “calladita” remark to Ada Colau, his lack of engagement in international affairs and the significance of his inability to speak English. The conversation also explores the PP's use of AI and social media to reach young voters, many of whom support Vox, and Santiago Abascal's decision to cancel his interview with Jordi Wild, a decision Carbonell describes as “a massive mistake”.
